title: FFO: reading REIT performance beyond net income
description: Understand the FFO bridge, per-share growth, and why adding back depreciation does not make buildings free to maintain.

sections.heading: What FFO measures
sections.text: Funds from operations is a supplemental performance measure for equity REITs. Nareit's definition starts with GAAP net income and makes specified adjustments for real estate depreciation, certain property disposal results, and qualifying impairments. The purpose is to make recurring real estate performance easier to interpret when historical-cost depreciation dominates accounting earnings. FFO is neither the cash-flow statement nor the amount legally required to be distributed. A mortgage REIT needs a different analytical framework because its main assets are loans or securities rather than depreciable buildings.

sections.heading: Use the bridge, then the share count
sections.text: Read each reconciliation line before accepting the headline. Distinguish Nareit FFO from management's additional measures labeled core, normalized, or adjusted FFO. Then ask whether the result belongs to common shareholders after preferred claims and noncontrolling interests. Aggregate growth can coexist with declining FFO per share when acquisitions require many new shares. Match annual performance with annual weighted-average diluted shares; a quarter-end share count can give a misleading result after a large issuance. For historical comparisons, keep ownership scope and reporting periods consistent.

sections.heading: Two useful, competing perspectives
sections.text: An operating perspective treats FFO as a cleaner starting point than earnings per share for comparing property businesses. A capital-preservation perspective asks what the add-back hides: roofs age, elevators need replacement, and tenants demand improvements. Both views can be useful. A growing FFO figure supported by healthy occupancy has different implications from growth accompanied by mounting deferred maintenance. Compare capital spending and leasing obligations separately instead of assuming that the accounting depreciation add-back makes all reported earnings economically distributable.

sections.heading: A source-reading workflow
sections.text: Open the issuer's annual filing and locate net income, its FFO reconciliation, diluted shares, the cash-flow statement, and capital commitments. Recreate the bridge for two periods and annotate changes in definitions. Use Nareit's guidance to understand the standard; use the issuer's notes to understand its application. Finally, explain any difference between FFO growth and operating cash-flow growth. Working capital, payment timing, and cash rent can create legitimate differences. Unexplained differences are a reason to read further, not proof of misconduct.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: earnings to FFO
example.text: Assume annual net income attributable to common shareholders is $40 million, qualifying real estate depreciation is $50 million, and a qualifying property sale gain is $10 million. Simplified FFO is 40 + 50 − 10 = $80 million. With 20 million diluted weighted-average shares, FFO is $4.00 per share. If the company spends $15 million maintaining buildings, that expenditure still matters even though this simplified FFO bridge does not deduct it. These invented figures omit other possible adjustments.

pitfall: Calling FFO cash available for dividends overlooks capital spending, financing needs, and working-capital movements.
checklist: Separate Nareit FFO from issuer adjustments.

title: AFFO: useful estimate, nonstandard definition
description: Learn to audit recurring cash adjustments and compare AFFO definitions before comparing payout ratios.

sections.heading: Why AFFO exists
sections.text: Adjusted funds from operations attempts to move from FFO toward a recurring economic earnings measure. Common adjustments address straight-line rent and recurring capital expenditure, but there is no universal AFFO definition. A label shared by two issuers does not guarantee comparable calculations. AFFO should therefore be read as a management-defined analytical estimate with a reconciliation, rather than a standardized cash balance. It can help frame dividend capacity, but cannot independently establish that a distribution is sustainable.

sections.heading: Inspect the difficult adjustments
sections.text: Sort adjustments into cash timing, recurring property investment, financing accounting, and claimed exceptional items. Straight-line rent can recognize revenue before the lease cash arrives. Tenant improvements and leasing commissions may be necessary to preserve occupancy even when paid irregularly. Stock compensation is noncash today but can dilute shareholders. An acquisition expense may be unusual for one business and routine for a serial acquirer. Write down which costs you would retain in a conservative view and show that alternative alongside the issuer's calculation.

sections.heading: Management's view and the owner's view
sections.text: Management may normalize volatile expenditures to make quarterly trends easier to understand. An owner may prefer actual cash spending because buildings cannot be maintained with an average estimate. Neither approach answers every question. Actual expenditure can spike during a refurbishment and understate a normal year; a smoothed reserve can miss a coming replacement cycle. Compare several years of actual maintenance and leasing spending with the deductions used in AFFO. Explain any persistent gap using property age, lease terms, and disclosed projects.

sections.heading: Read definitions before rankings
sections.text: Start with the issuer's net-income reconciliation, then read every footnote attached to AFFO. Compare the latest definition with the prior year's definition, not just the numbers. Check whether joint ventures, preferred dividends, and diluted shares are treated consistently. Return to the cash-flow statement to identify expenditures outside the measure and to the liquidity section for funding commitments. A cross-company table should include a definitions column. When material adjustments differ, compare your own clearly labeled sensitivity calculations instead of presenting the headline ratios as perfectly equivalent.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: two reasonable views
example.text: Suppose FFO is $100 million. Deduct $8 million of straight-line rent and $12 million of recurring property expenditure to obtain simplified AFFO of $80 million. If the issuer also adds back $4 million of stock compensation, its reported version becomes $84 million. A $60 million common dividend is 75% of the first figure and approximately 71.4% of the second. Neither ratio changes the cash dividend; the different denominators explain the difference. This invented example is a sensitivity exercise, not an issuer definition.

pitfall: A lower published AFFO payout ratio can result from a more permissive adjustment policy rather than a safer dividend.
checklist: Compare maintenance deductions with actual spending.

title: NOI: separate the property from its financing
description: Build a property operating view and understand why positive NOI does not guarantee positive shareholder cash flow.

sections.heading: The property-level question
sections.text: Net operating income asks what a property earns after its operating expenses, before the financing and corporate layers. A simple model subtracts property taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, and other property operating costs from property revenue. Issuer definitions can vary, including treatment of straight-line rent and particular reimbursements. NOI is useful because two identical buildings should not appear operationally different simply because one owner borrowed more. It does not represent the income available to common shareholders after all obligations.

sections.heading: Trace revenues and expenses together
sections.text: A gross lease may show substantial tenant reimbursements and substantial reimbursable expenses. A net lease can leave many obligations directly with the tenant. Comparing revenue margins without understanding those structures can mislead. Read who actually bears taxes, insurance, repairs, and capital replacements. Also separate billed rent from collected rent, contractual rent from concessions, and occupied space from paying space. A favorable revenue trend can conceal a larger insurance increase or a temporary reimbursement settlement that will not recur.

sections.heading: Growth and quality are different questions
sections.text: An expansion-minded reader may celebrate total NOI growth because new acquisitions add income. An operating reader asks whether the existing portfolio improved without acquisitions. Both are legitimate, but answer different questions. Same-store analysis helps isolate an eligible comparable pool, while total NOI explains the current enterprise. Neither captures all capital required to maintain the income stream. A landlord may sustain NOI by spending heavily on tenant improvements outside property operating expense. Review the cost of maintaining occupancy as well as the occupancy itself.

sections.heading: How to reconstruct the story
sections.text: Find the property operating table and its reconciliation in the supplemental report or filing. List included revenue and expense categories and note cash versus accounting presentation. Build a bridge from prior-period NOI using rent, occupancy, expenses, acquisitions, dispositions, and currency. Then connect NOI to corporate expenses, interest, and recurring investment. This second bridge makes clear why healthy buildings can belong to a financially stressed owner. Use a full year and comparable seasons when utility expenses or occupancy vary sharply across quarters.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: NOI is only the first layer
example.text: Imagine annual rent and reimbursements of $12 million and property operating expenses of $4 million. NOI is $8 million. Interest of $3 million, allocated corporate costs of $1 million, and recurring capital needs of $2 million leave $2 million before other cash movements and obligations. If property expenses rise 10% while revenue stays flat, NOI falls to $7.6 million: a 5% decline. The effect on the simplified residual is a 20% decline, from $2 million to $1.6 million.

pitfall: Treating NOI as free cash flow skips financing, corporate overhead, capital expenditure, and other claims.
checklist: Read the NOI definition and reconciliation.
Bridge property income to owner cash needs.

title: NAV: an estimate with assumptions, not a price promise
description: Construct a simple net asset value bridge and test how debt and capitalization rates change the result.

sections.heading: The estimate behind the acronym
sections.text: Net asset value estimates the current value of assets after subtracting liabilities and senior claims. For an equity REIT, an analyst often values stabilized properties using income and capitalization rates, then separately considers development, land, cash, and other businesses. Dividing common equity value by an appropriate diluted share count produces NAV per share. This is an estimate, not an executable sale offer. Accounting book value follows a different purpose and should not be silently substituted for estimated market value.

sections.heading: Build a transparent asset bridge
sections.text: Group properties by economically meaningful factors such as geography, sector, lease duration, and condition. Apply an explicitly stated income period and cap-rate range to each group. Add nonoperating assets separately and avoid valuing a development both as completed income and as construction in progress. Subtract debt, preferred equity, relevant liabilities, and minority interests consistently. Joint ventures require particular care: proportionate income should be matched with proportionate assets and debt. A beautifully precise spreadsheet cannot correct a mismatched ownership basis.

sections.heading: Why a discount may persist
sections.text: An asset-focused investor may see a share price below estimated NAV as an attractive entry. A skeptical investor may see outdated property assumptions, large refurbishment needs, taxes, transaction costs, or weak capital allocation. A premium can reflect expected growth or operating capabilities, but can also reflect optimistic pricing. A discount alone does not identify which interpretation is correct. Ask what observable event could close it, what costs that event would involve, and whether selling assets would leave the remaining portfolio weaker.

sections.heading: Read evidence and show a range
sections.text: Start with property income, debt notes, ownership disclosures, and development commitments in issuer filings. Compare assumptions with disclosed transactions that genuinely resemble the properties under review; headline averages from another sector are weak evidence. State the valuation date and distinguish trailing from forward income. Present a sensitivity grid rather than one authoritative-looking number. If recent comparable transactions are sparse, widen the range and say why. NAV sensitivity is a way to expose assumptions, not a forecast that the stock will converge to your estimate.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: leverage amplifies uncertainty
example.text: Assume stabilized NOI of $60 million, a 6% cap rate, $20 million cash, $400 million debt, and 20 million shares, with no other claims. Property value is $1 billion and NAV is ($1,000m + $20m − $400m) / 20m = $31 per share. At a 7% cap rate, property value falls to about $857.1 million and NAV to about $23.86. A one-percentage-point cap-rate change reduces this simplified equity estimate by roughly 23%.

pitfall: A share-price discount to estimated NAV is not a guaranteed return or a guaranteed liquidation value.
checklist: State the date and income period.
Include senior claims and development commitments.

title: Cap rates: reading income, price, and risk together
description: Understand the cap-rate equation, differences from dividend yield, and the limits of acquisition spreads.

sections.heading: A pricing ratio for property income
sections.text: A capitalization rate relates a property's NOI to its price or estimated value. Dividing income by price produces the rate; dividing income by an assumed rate produces an estimated value. Keep trailing and forward income distinct. The ratio describes a property before the owner's financing structure and does not equal a REIT shareholder's dividend yield or total return. A high cap rate may reflect more income per dollar paid, but the durability and future cost of that income still require investigation.

sections.heading: Make comparisons economically similar
sections.text: Before comparing two advertised rates, ask whether both use the same income period, occupancy assumption, reserve policy, and transaction-cost treatment. A stabilized warehouse and a half-empty office building are not comparable merely because both have annual rent. Tenant credit, local supply, remaining lease term, capital needs, and rent relative to the market can change the interpretation. A seller's projected NOI may depend on renewals or expense savings not yet achieved. Recalculate using a clearly identified current-income case as well as the projection.

sections.heading: The acquisition-spread debate
sections.text: A buyer may highlight the spread between an acquisition cap rate and borrowing cost. That spread can be informative, but debt is not the only capital source and interest is not the only cost. Corporate overhead, equity issuance, leasing investment, and transaction expenses also matter. The optimistic view emphasizes contractual increases and operating improvements. The skeptical view asks whether the initial yield compensates for tenant failure or obsolescence. Examine both the first-year economics and a stressed renewal period before describing a purchase as accretive.

sections.heading: Build and verify a sensitivity table
sections.text: Read an issuer's transaction announcement and supplemental disclosures for how acquisition yield is defined. Compare those disclosures with the financial filing's lease and expense policies. Use a table that varies both NOI and cap rate, since weak income and higher required returns can occur together. Keep the calculation separate from a forecast. Small rate changes can materially alter value, and a valuation based on an assumed rate is not evidence that buyers will actually pay that price in a difficult market.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: the same income, different prices
example.text: A property generating $5 million of annual NOI at a $100 million purchase price has a 5% cap rate. If buyers require 6% for the same income, the implied value is $5 million / 0.06, or approximately $83.33 million. If NOI also falls 10% to $4.5 million, the implied value at 6% becomes $75 million. These examples ignore transaction costs and future spending. They illustrate the formula, not a predicted market move or an investment recommendation.

pitfall: Subtracting an interest rate from a cap rate does not calculate the shareholder's total return.
checklist: Check whether NOI is achieved or projected.
Include future leasing and capital costs.
Stress income and cap rate together.

title: Payout ratios: choose the denominator before judging safety
description: Compare FFO and AFFO coverage without confusing dividend policy with the REIT taxable-income distribution requirement.

sections.heading: A ratio with more than one denominator
sections.text: A payout ratio divides dividends by an earnings or cash-generation measure. For property REITs, investors often examine FFO or AFFO payout ratios because GAAP earnings include real estate depreciation. These ratios answer different questions and can differ materially. Write the denominator in the label rather than saying only payout ratio. Use common dividends with income available to common shareholders, and match annual dividends to annual performance. A quarterly dividend annualized today is a forward assumption, not the same as dividends actually paid last year.

sections.heading: The tax rule is a separate calculation
sections.text: The commonly cited U.S. REIT distribution requirement concerns at least 90% of qualifying taxable income, subject to the applicable tax rules. It does not mean a REIT must distribute 90% of FFO, AFFO, revenue, or market value. Taxable income and financial reporting measures can diverge. This educational distinction does not determine an individual investor's tax treatment. For a company's compliance discussion, read its tax section and distribution disclosures rather than reverse-engineering compliance from the AFFO payout ratio.

sections.heading: Coverage versus reinvestment flexibility
sections.text: An income-focused reader may prefer a larger distribution today. A balance-sheet-focused reader may prefer retaining more funds to repair properties, repay debt, or avoid issuing shares. A lower ratio creates potential room but does not guarantee good capital allocation. A higher ratio can be manageable when cash flows are stable and investment needs are limited, yet leave little margin for a tenant default. Evaluate the ratio alongside the business model, recurring expenditure, debt calendar, and available liquidity rather than applying one universal safety cutoff.

sections.heading: A practical reading and stress workflow
sections.text: Collect declared and paid common dividends, the issuer's FFO and AFFO reconciliations, and diluted share information. Separate special dividends from the ordinary run rate. Review whether AFFO excludes costs you consider recurring. Calculate coverage under both the reported measure and a conservative alternative. Then reduce income and increase interest costs in a simple sensitivity exercise. Check the board's declared distribution language: a historical payment pattern does not bind future decisions. Revisit the analysis when financing or lease conditions change.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: coverage under pressure
example.text: Assume annual ordinary dividends of $3 per share, FFO of $4.50, and AFFO of $4.00. FFO payout is 66.7%; AFFO payout is 75%. If AFFO declines 20% to $3.20 while the dividend stays $3, the AFFO ratio rises to 93.75%. At $2.80 AFFO it becomes 107.1%. This does not mechanically predict a cut, but it shows that the dividend would exceed this measure of recurring earnings. No taxable-income figure is supplied, so tax compliance cannot be inferred.

pitfall: The 90% REIT taxable-income rule is not an FFO or AFFO payout target.
checklist: Stress both earnings and financing costs.

title: Debt maturities: read the calendar, not just the average
description: Map refinancing needs against cash, committed liquidity, lease risk, and future borrowing costs.

sections.heading: Why timing can dominate the debt ratio
sections.text: Debt maturity analysis asks when principal must be repaid or refinanced. Two REITs with the same debt balance and current interest expense can face very different risks if one has a large repayment next year and the other has staggered obligations. A weighted-average maturity compresses that calendar into a single figure and can hide a near-term concentration. Read the annual buckets and material individual facilities. Include mortgage debt, unsecured notes, revolving credit, and the appropriate share of joint-venture obligations.

sections.heading: Map the available funding sources
sections.text: Compare upcoming principal with unrestricted cash, committed undrawn credit, retained operating funds, and realistically available asset-sale proceeds. A credit line can bridge a repayment but may itself mature soon, require covenant compliance, or carry floating rates. An asset sale is an assumption until completed and may reduce future income. Do not treat restricted cash as freely available or count the same facility twice. Read extension options carefully: the borrower may have to satisfy conditions, pay a fee, or maintain specified financial ratios.

sections.heading: Refinancing success can still reduce earnings
sections.text: The optimistic case is that a sound borrower can refinance well before maturity and retain access to multiple capital markets. The cautious case recognizes that access and price are separate questions. Replacing cheap debt with more expensive debt can lower per-share earnings even when principal is fully refinanced. Selling assets or issuing equity may protect liquidity while changing future growth. Evaluate the cost of each route. A debt maturity is not automatically a crisis, but treating every maturity as costless is equally unhelpful.

sections.heading: A filing-based review
sections.text: Begin with the debt footnote, then read liquidity, covenant disclosures, hedging notes, and events after the reporting date. Place maturities and hedge expirations on one timeline. Identify secured assets that cannot easily support another borrowing and distinguish fixed from floating exposure after hedges. Compare the financing calendar with major lease expirations and development payments. Use issuer investor materials as an index, then verify details in filed documents. Date the analysis because a bond issuance completed after year-end can materially change the picture.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: refinancing at a higher rate
example.text: Suppose $200 million of debt carrying 3% interest matures next year. Refinancing the full amount at an assumed 6% increases annual interest from $6 million to $12 million, a $6 million difference before fees or hedging. Across 30 million shares, that is $0.20 per share before other effects. If the company repays $50 million first, the new $150 million borrowing costs $9 million annually. The repayment uses liquidity and should not be modeled as free money.

pitfall: An attractive average maturity can conceal one large near-term repayment and an expiring credit facility.
checklist: Check extension conditions and covenant headroom.
Model higher rates and lower asset-sale proceeds.

title: Interest coverage: test the earnings cushion
description: Understand coverage ratios, covenant definitions, and why principal repayments require a separate check.

sections.heading: Which earnings cover which charges?
sections.text: Interest coverage compares an earnings measure with interest expense. The numerator may be EBIT, EBITDA, EBITDAre, or an issuer-adjusted amount; the denominator may include different financing costs. Fixed-charge coverage can add obligations such as preferred distributions or other specified charges. Debt-service coverage can include principal obligations depending on its definition. These labels are not interchangeable. Copy the exact formula before comparing issuers or judging compliance with a covenant. A rounded presentation in a slide deck may omit important contractual qualifications.

sections.heading: The limits of a backward-looking ratio
sections.text: A trailing ratio describes a past period. It may not include a full year of higher interest on newly refinanced debt, a tenant bankruptcy after the reporting date, or a completed acquisition's income. Conversely, temporary disruption may depress historical results even when signed leases support recovery. Prepare a clearly labeled forward sensitivity using disclosed changes and explicit assumptions. Do not mix a forward numerator with a trailing denominator without explanation. Capitalized interest also deserves attention because construction financing costs may not appear in the same place as expensed interest.

sections.heading: Operational cushion versus liquidity
sections.text: A lender may emphasize contractual coverage because it governs borrowing rights. An equity investor may emphasize recurring cash after maintenance because that supports dividends and reinvestment. Both views matter, and neither replaces the maturity calendar. Strong coverage does not ensure cash to repay a large principal amount tomorrow. Weak coverage does not alone reveal the amount of unrestricted cash on hand. Read coverage, leverage, liquidity, and maturities together to understand whether the problem is earnings pressure, refinancing timing, or both.

sections.heading: Read the covenant, not a universal cutoff
sections.text: Locate the debt agreement or filing description and identify calculation periods, permitted adjustments, cure provisions, and minimum requirements. Compare the issuer's reported covenant calculation with its investor-facing performance ratio; the formulas may differ. Then calculate headroom under a lower-income and higher-rate case. Note that compliance today is not a promise of future borrowing availability. Where an agreement is unclear, describe the uncertainty instead of inventing a threshold. Cross-company comparisons should preserve these definition differences in the table.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: a two-sided stress
example.text: Assume the chosen annual earnings measure is $120 million and interest is $30 million. Coverage is 4.0 times. A 15% earnings decline reduces the numerator to $102 million, while refinancing raises interest to $40 million. Coverage falls to 2.55 times. If a hypothetical covenant minimum were 2.0 times under exactly the same formula, the company would remain above it in this example. That says nothing about actual issuer covenants, scheduled principal payments, or dividend capacity.

pitfall: Comparing ratios with different numerator adjustments or treating interest coverage as cash available for debt principal produces false comfort.
checklist: Separate operating metrics from legal covenant tests.

title: Dilution: follow your share of the business
description: Distinguish a rising share count from harmful economic dilution and evaluate acquisition growth per share.

sections.heading: More shares do not answer the whole question
sections.text: Issuing common stock increases the number of ownership claims. Whether it improves or weakens the economics of each existing share depends on the price received, issuance costs, and use of proceeds. REITs may raise equity to buy properties, fund development, or reduce debt. Total assets and total FFO can rise while FFO per share falls. Start with the per-share result, then examine risk and future investment requirements. A larger company is not automatically a better investment for each owner.

sections.heading: Separate earnings and asset-value effects
sections.text: An issuance can be accretive to a short-term earnings measure yet unfavorable under a particular NAV estimate, or the reverse. Earnings accretion depends on the incremental return after financing and operating costs. NAV impact depends on the assumed asset values and issue price. Because NAV itself is uncertain, present this analysis as a scenario. Also consider whether the transaction reduces leverage, broadens tenants, or creates execution risk. One numerical measure cannot summarize every change in the shareholder's position.

sections.heading: Growth and resilience can conflict
sections.text: A growth-focused management team may emphasize acquisitions made possible by fresh capital. An existing holder may question why stock was issued at a depressed price. Sometimes raising equity protects the business against expensive refinancing, even when near-term per-share earnings decline. Sometimes appealing acquisition headlines conceal weak returns. Evaluate the alternative funding choices and their risks. Ask whether the benefit is visible in durable per-share income, improved financing flexibility, or a credible project schedule rather than assuming every share issuance is either harmful or beneficial.

sections.heading: Follow the filing trail
sections.text: Read the equity note, cash-flow financing section, stock-compensation disclosure, and earnings reconciliation. Distinguish shares issued during the period, end-period shares, and weighted-average diluted shares used for reported earnings. Include relevant convertible instruments and operating-partnership units consistently. For a transaction, check the pro forma period and whether acquired earnings are annualized while issuance costs are excluded. Compare management's accretion expectation with later reported results, allowing for timing and unexpected operating changes. Keep your original assumptions so you can explain the difference.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: total growth, per-share decline
example.text: A REIT earns $100 million of annual FFO on 25 million shares, or $4 per share. It issues 5 million shares and adds $15 million of annual FFO after the modeled costs. Total FFO increases 15% to $115 million, but the share count rises 20% to 30 million. FFO per share becomes about $3.83, a 4.2% decline. Adding $25 million instead would produce about $4.17 per share. These simplified full-year cases ignore transaction timing and other adjustments.

pitfall: Judging a transaction by total FFO growth ignores how many additional shares claim that income.
checklist: Match income timing with weighted shares.
Consider leverage and realistic funding alternatives.

title: Lease expirations: the calendar behind rental income
description: Read lease rollover exposure, renewal economics, downtime, and why long leases can be both protection and a constraint.

sections.heading: A lease schedule is an income-risk map
sections.text: Lease expirations show when contracted rental arrangements come up for renewal or replacement. Exposure can be measured by rent, area, or property count; each weighting tells a different story. Rent weighting highlights income at stake, while area can reveal the physical amount of space to re-lease. A weighted-average lease term is useful but can hide a concentrated expiry year. Read annual buckets, major tenants, break options, and renewal rights. A stated final expiry date may not capture every route to an earlier income change.

sections.heading: Renewal economics go beyond the rent increase
sections.text: A positive rental spread compares new and old rent under the issuer's definition, but it does not automatically measure the full return on renewal. Free rent, tenant improvements, commissions, and downtime can offset a higher headline rent. Cash and straight-line spreads may differ. Retaining a tenant at a modest increase can produce better near-term cash economics than replacing it at a large advertised increase after a long vacancy. Compare total lease economics over a consistent period rather than celebrating the percentage alone.

sections.heading: Long leases offer protection and tradeoffs
sections.text: A stability-focused reader values long contractual income and limited near-term rollover. A growth-focused reader may prefer shorter leases when market rents are rising quickly. Long leases can delay repricing, and contractual protection depends on tenant ability to pay. Short leases can reset income faster but expose the owner to weaker market rents and repeated leasing costs. The relevant question is how lease length fits the sector, tenant credit, market supply, and balance sheet. No single average duration is universally best.

sections.heading: Connect leases to the financing calendar
sections.text: Find the expiration table in the annual filing or supplemental report, then read tenant concentration, rent-collection, occupancy, and leasing-cost disclosures. Identify whether renewal options are included and how annualized rent is defined. Compare the largest rollover years with debt maturities and development obligations. A company facing both major lease uncertainty and refinancing may have less flexibility than either table suggests alone. Track completed renewals over time, distinguishing signed leases from commenced leases. Do not assume that every expired lease becomes vacant or that every tenant renews.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: headline rent versus cash received
example.text: Suppose an expiring lease paid $1 million annually. A replacement lease promises $1.1 million annually, a 10% increase. If the building sits empty for six months before the new lease begins, first-year rent is only $550,000, before free-rent incentives or leasing costs. Add $200,000 of tenant improvements and commissions, and the first-year cash effect is much weaker than the rental spread suggests. Over later years the higher rent may help recover those costs, depending on lease duration and collections.

pitfall: A positive renewal spread does not account automatically for vacancy time, concessions, or capital spent to secure the tenant.
checklist: Identify whether exposure is rent- or area-weighted.
Compare cash and accounting rent spreads.
Overlay lease and debt maturity calendars.

title: Same-store NOI: test growth inside the existing portfolio
description: Understand comparable-property pools, cash versus accounting growth, and the exclusions that can change the story.

sections.heading: What the comparable pool solves
sections.text: Same-store NOI compares a defined set of properties across periods to reduce distortion from acquisitions and dispositions. It helps answer whether an existing operating portfolio improved. The phrase does not describe one universal pool: issuers set eligibility rules for ownership duration, stabilization, redevelopment, and other conditions. Read the population definition before comparing growth rates. A same-store result may cover only part of the economic business and should sit beside total property income, not replace it.

sections.heading: Look underneath the growth percentage
sections.text: Break the movement into rental rates, occupancy, concessions, bad debt, reimbursements, and operating expenses. Cash measures can differ from accounting measures because of straight-line rent and other noncash items. Currency translation and ownership changes can also affect multinational or joint-venture portfolios. A percentage becomes more informative when the company explains these drivers. Strong rent growth can coexist with weaker occupancy, while lower property taxes can temporarily improve NOI despite flat demand. Distinguish repeatable operating improvements from unusually easy comparisons.

sections.heading: Comparable does not mean complete
sections.text: An operational view values a stable pool because it separates management of existing buildings from acquisition spending. A skeptical view asks whether exclusions remove the hardest properties. Redevelopment exclusions can be reasonable when a building changes substantially, but they also mean the metric omits part of the owner's risk and capital needs. Examine excluded assets separately rather than declaring the metric invalid. Review the percentage of total NOI represented by the pool and changes in membership across years. A shrinking pool deserves an explanation.

sections.heading: A reproducible reading workflow
sections.text: Download the supplemental report, locate the population footnote, and record both current and comparison-period NOI. Check whether results are consolidated, proportionate, or reported at full venture ownership. Recalculate the growth rate and compare cash with accounting versions. Then build a short driver note and a list of exclusions. For cross-company comparisons, preserve differences in sector and definitions. Finally, connect the operating result with recurring capital expenditure: stronger same-store NOI does not disclose what was spent outside operating expense to obtain it.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: acquisitions mask a decline
example.text: An eligible same-store pool produces $50 million NOI last year and $49 million this year, a 2% decline. Newly acquired properties add $10 million, taking total NOI from $50 million to $59 million, an 18% increase in this simplified case. Both statements are true: the enterprise is larger and the comparable pool weakened. If management excludes a redevelopment property, analyze its income loss and project spending separately rather than quietly adding it to one side of the comparison.

pitfall: Comparing same-store growth without checking pool eligibility, ownership share, and cash adjustments can produce a false ranking.
checklist: Examine excluded properties and capital spending.

title: Dividend cuts: analyze the funding gap before the yield
description: Build a dividend stress review using recurring earnings, liquidity, debt repayments, and board disclosures.

sections.heading: A dividend is a capital-allocation decision
sections.text: A REIT dividend depends on operating results, financing conditions, legal requirements, and board decisions. A long payment record can provide context but does not guarantee future payments. The U.S. distribution requirement relates to taxable income, not a fixed dividend per share or 90% of AFFO. If taxable income falls, that rule does not preserve the previous cash distribution. Analyze ordinary dividends separately from special distributions tied to events such as asset sales, because their recurrence and funding sources can differ.

sections.heading: Look for converging pressures
sections.text: One weak quarter rarely provides a complete answer. A more useful review asks whether recurring coverage is deteriorating while debt maturities, leasing costs, or tenant problems consume cash. Check AFFO definitions, operating cash flow, unrestricted liquidity, and future capital commitments. Borrowing or asset sales can support payments temporarily, but their costs and effect on future income matter. A high indicated yield can result from a falling share price while the displayed dividend still reflects an old run rate. Verify the latest declaration rather than relying on a static quote.

sections.heading: A cut can protect the enterprise and hurt the owner
sections.text: An income-dependent holder experiences a cut as an immediate loss of expected cash. A balance-sheet perspective may see retained funds as a way to reduce financing risk or preserve valuable properties. Both consequences can occur at once. It is also possible for a cut to be insufficient if the underlying business continues to weaken. Avoid automatically labeling every reduction either a buying opportunity or proof of permanent failure. The relevant analysis compares the post-cut cash budget with realistic operating and financing scenarios.

sections.heading: A source-led monitoring process
sections.text: Read the latest dividend declaration, annual and quarterly liquidity discussions, debt covenant disclosures, and material events filed after the reporting period. Track per-share coverage and the actual cash budget rather than a single yield threshold. Record management's assumptions and distinguish guidance from commitments. If income information is incomplete, publish scenarios with explicit limits instead of assigning a false probability of a cut. Recheck after major tenant events, refinancing, or asset sales because these can change both near-term liquidity and the ongoing earnings base.

example.heading: Hypothetical arithmetic: a cut releases cash but does not fix everything
example.text: Assume 40 million shares and an annual dividend of $2.40 per share: total annual payments are $96 million. Reducing the run rate to $1.80 lowers payments to $72 million, retaining $24 million annually before timing effects. If the company faces a $100 million funding gap, the change alone does not fill it. If the share price is $20, the indicated yield falls from 12% to 9%, assuming that price stays unchanged. Actual prices can move, and neither yield predicts total return.

pitfall: A very high displayed yield may use an obsolete dividend assumption and does not establish a sustainable income stream.
checklist: Verify the latest declared ordinary dividend.
Check recurring coverage and cash funding separately.
Overlay debt, lease, and capital commitments.
Evaluate the post-cut budget rather than the headline alone.
